resident.chief_complaint: Weakness and numbness involving all four extremities and progressive sphincter dysfunction over the last 2 months in a 41-year-old female with no history of trauma.
resident.history: A 41-year-old female with no history of trauma presented with weakness and numbness involving all four extremities and progressive sphincter dysfunction over the last 2 months. Initial cervical noncontrast MRI showed a hyperintense intramedullary cord signal, with differential diagnoses including cervical spondylotic myelopathy and tumor. She was referred for an open biopsy of the cervical spinal cord to document the pathology of the tumor. At the time of transfer, she had severe spastic quadriparesis, markedly greater in the upper than in the lower extremities. Follow-up MRI revealed cervical spondylosis with C5–C6 and C6–C7 cord compression associated with an extensive intramedullary high cord signal and cord enlargement on T2-weighted sagittal images extending from C5 to C7; axial images confirmed the intramedullary signal abnormality. T1-weighted MRI sagittal scan showed the lesion enhanced with contrast at the C5–C6 level.
resident.physical_exam: On examination at the time of transfer, severe spastic quadriparesis was present, markedly greater in the upper than in the lower extremities. red_flags.finding: Intramedullary cord enlargement and contrast enhancement at C5–C6 on MRI
red_flags.rationale: This suggests an intrinsic cord lesion (e.g., tumor, demyelination, inflammation) that could independently cause the progressive myelopathy; surgical decompression for spondylotic compression may not address the primary pathology, and biopsy or medical management may be needed.

In compressive cervical myelopathy from C5–C7 spondylosis, lower extremities are typically more affected due to longer corticospinal tracts; upper extremity predominance suggests a central cord or intramedullary process, reinforcing the likelihood of a primary cord lesion rather than compression alone.

neurology.symptom_imaging_mismatch: The imaging shows C5–C6 and C6–C7 cord compression, but the clinical pattern of upper extremity-predominant spastic quadriparesis is atypical for compressive cervical myelopathy at those levels, which would be expected to affect lower limbs more; additionally, cord enlargement and contrast enhancement are not typical for simple spondylotic compression, suggesting an intramedullary lesion that better explains the symptoms.

physiatrist_opening.public_message: I remain the strongest advocate for conservative care. Given the progressive myelopathy and sphincter dysfunction, surgery is being considered, but before proceeding to irreversible intervention, I propose a formal, time-limited 3-6 month trial of intensive conservative management under close neurological monitoring. This would include supervised physical therapy for gait/balance/strength, occupational therapy for activities of daily living, cervical isometric strengthening, posture education, and avoidance of high-risk activities. The literature on nonoperative management of cervical spondylotic myelopathy reports that a subset of patients—particularly those with mild symptoms and no rapid progression—can stabilize or improve without surgery; however, I acknowledge that severe spastic quadriparesis with sphincter involvement and cord enhancement indicates a poorer prognosis for conservative care. Therefore, I define failure as any of the following: (1) no improvement or further deterioration in motor or sphincter function after 3 months of strict conservative therapy; (2) new or worsening neurological deficits during the trial; (3) progression of intramedullary signal abnormality or enhancement on follow-up MRI at 3 months; or (4) inability to participate in therapy due to pain or functional decline. If any of these occur, I will accept that conservative management has failed and support surgical intervention or biopsy as appropriate. Until then, I hold my stance for a trial of conservative care.

vice_opinions.assessment: This is a 41-year-old woman with progressive severe cervical myelopathy and sphincter dysfunction over 2 months. Imaging demonstrates C5-C6 and C6-C7 spondylotic compression with cord signal change, cord enlargement, and focal contrast enhancement. The enhancement and enlargement raise concern for an intrinsic cord lesion (tumor or inflammation), but they can also occur with acute/subacute compressive myelopathy. Given the rapid progression, sphincter involvement, and severe quadriparesis, urgent surgical intervention is warranted. A 3-6 month conservative trial is not appropriate; this patient meets criteria for failure of conservative management at presentation.
proposed_options: Urgent anterior cervical decompression and fusion (ACDF) at C5-C6 and C6-C7, with intraoperative neuromonitoring; obtain postoperative MRI in 4-6 weeks to assess resolution of enhancement/enlargement.
Posterior cervical decompression with laminectomy/fusion and simultaneous biopsy of the intramedullary lesion if the compression can be adequately addressed posteriorly.

Upfront tissue diagnosis via open biopsy or CT-guided needle biopsy of the enhancing intramedullary lesion before decompression, followed by staged decompression if pathology is not definitively non-surgical.
vice_opinions.preferred_option: Urgent anterior cervical decompression and fusion (ACDF) at C5-C6 and C6-C7, with intraoperative neuromonitoring; obtain postoperative MRI in 4-6 weeks to assess resolution of enhancement/enlargement.
disagreement_points: The recommendation for a 3-6 month conservative trial is not supported by evidence and risks irreversible loss; I oppose delaying surgery.
The optimal sequence of tissue diagnosis versus decompression is uncertain; I favor decompression first, but biopsy may be needed if enhancement persists.
Lack of documented past medical history and laboratory results limits assessment for infectious/inflammatory causes; these should be obtained urgently.
deferred_questions_to_director: Do you agree with proceeding to urgent decompression without a preoperative tissue diagnosis, given the atypical enhancement?
Should we perform additional imaging (e.g., CT myelogram, dynamic flexion-extension films) to evaluate stability?
Is there any contraindication to surgery from undocumented comorbidities that we should clarify before booking?

I defer final decision on biopsy timing to the director.

vice_opinions.assessment: The patient has severe progressive cervical myelopathy with sphincter dysfunction, cord compression at C5-C6 and C6-C7, and an enhancing intramedullary lesion. While the enhancing lesion raises the possibility of intrinsic cord pathology, the clinical picture is highly suggestive of compressive myelopathy, and the enhancement may reflect myelomalacia or edema from compression. The requested workup is reasonable to clarify the diagnosis, but it should be expedited and not become a conservative management trial; the risk of irreversible neurological worsening increases with delay. I continue to view urgent surgical decompression as indicated if compressive myelopathy is confirmed, and I do not support a 3-6 month trial of conservative care.
proposed_options: Expedited diagnostic workup (airway assessment, dynamic MRI/CT myelogram, CSF/serum studies, neurology history) with reassessment within 72 hours; if compressive myelopathy is confirmed or remains the leading diagnosis, proceed to ACDF C5-C7 (or posterior decompression/fusion if anterior anatomy contraindicated) without a conservative trial.
If workup suggests intrinsic cord lesion (tumor/inflammatory), obtain neuro-oncology/medical spine consultation and plan for biopsy with possible decompression if mass effect is present.
Continue physiatry for perioperative optimization, respiratory support, and rehabilitation planning, but not as a standalone conservative management arm.
vice_opinions.preferred_option: Expedited diagnostic workup with early surgical decompression if compressive myelopathy confirmed.
disagreement_points: I do not support a 3-6 month conservative trial in this patient; progressive sphincter dysfunction and severe quadriparesis are red flags for rapid deterioration, and the literature on conservative management of severe myelopathy shows poor outcomes.

The enhancing lesion should not automatically be assumed to be intrinsic cord pathology; it can be caused by venous congestion, edema, or myelomalacia from chronic compression, and waiting for exhaustive workup before addressing compression risks permanent cord injury.
Airway evaluation is important but should not delay surgical decision-making; it can be completed urgently and may be optimized perioperatively.
deferred_questions_to_director: What is the maximum acceptable timeframe for the requested workup and reassembly before deciding on surgery? I recommend no more than 72 hours.
If the workup does not confirm intrinsic cord pathology but imaging shows persistent or dynamic cord compression, will you authorize decompression without a formal conservative trial?
If CSF/serum studies are negative and imaging remains ambiguous, should we proceed with decompression, biopsy, or continue observation? I recommend a surgical option given the severity.
